content: Children and adolescents who exhibit symptoms of tuberculosis (TB) or have been exposed to TB may benefit from family-centered, integrated services in addition to standard TB care. This recommendation is conditional and based on evidence of very low certainty. Decentralized TB services, which bring care closer to the community, are recommended for settings with limited access to healthcare or high TB prevalence. However, decentralization should not replace specialized pediatric TB services at higher levels of the health system. Family-centered approaches are encouraged as an additional option to standard TB services, particularly in settings where integration with other health programs is limited. This approach emphasizes the importance of family involvement in care at all levels of the health system. Treatment support provided by trained lay providers or healthcare workers is preferred over support from family members or unsupported treatment. Video-supported treatment may be used when video communication technology is available and can be effectively managed by healthcare providers and patients. Interventions should be tailored to individual needs, available resources, and implementation conditions. Options for treatment support include video-supported treatment, communityor home-based support, and regular follow-up. Decentralization of TB services involves providing diagnostic and treatment services at lower levels of the health system, such as primary healthcare or community levels. This approach improves access to care, reduces time and financial burdens for families, and enhances continuity of care. It also fosters community support, which can improve treatment adherence and address barriers such as transportation costs, school absences, and income loss. For effective implementation, national TB programs (NTPs) should assess the feasibility of decentralization and integration of TB services based on local disease burden, resources, and infrastructure. Stakeholder engagement, including consultations with relevant programs and professional bodies, is essential to identify opportunities and address challenges. A skilled healthcare workforce is critical for delivering high-quality TB services. Capacity-building efforts, including training, task-shifting, and supportive supervision, are necessary to equip staff with the skills to manage pediatric TB effectively. Health facilities should have access to diagnostic supplies and child-friendly TB medications. Decentralization also requires strengthening health information systems for data collection and analysis. The socioeconomic impact of TB on children, adolescents, and their families is significant, often exacerbating poverty and social deprivation. TB in a family can lead to school dropouts, income loss, and disrupted growth and development in children. Family-centered care models and integrated services can help reduce the socioeconomic burden of TB while improving treatment outcomes. Country experiences in implementing decentralized, family-centered TB services highlight the feasibility of these approaches across different healthcare levels. For example, task-shifting pediatric TB screening to lay healthcare workers has been successful and well-accepted. Training and supervision programs targeting frontline healthcare workers are essential for building confidence and capacity to diagnose and manage pediatric TB effectively. In summary, decentralized, family-centered, and integrated TB services are recommended to improve access to care, reduce the socioeconomic impact of TB, and enhance treatment outcomes for children and adolescents. These services should complement, rather than replace, specialized TB care at higher levels of the health system.
